client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last month. There's this coffee shop she loved, and every time I end up near it — or even think about going in — I just get hit with this wave of sadness that I can't shake. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how I feel, but I figured I should try something because it's starting to affect my daily routine.
therapist: Thank you for being here and for taking that brave step to try, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — that ambivalence makes complete sense, and it's actually really common when we're grieving. It sounds like the coffee shop has become a powerful place that holds a lot of love for your grandmother, and that wave of sadness you feel is your heart recognizing how much she meant to you. I'd love to understand a little more — when that wave hits, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind in that moment?

client: When that wave hits, I usually think something like... "I should have visited her more" or "Why didn't I call her that last week when I had the chance." It's like my brain immediately goes to all the things I did wrong or didn't do enough of, and then I just feel this crushing guilt on top of the sadness. I know logically she knew I loved her, but in that moment it doesn't feel that way at all.
therapist: That crushing guilt layered on top of the grief sounds so heavy to carry, and it makes a lot of sense that your mind goes searching for reasons or things to "fix" — that's actually a very common way our brains try to cope with a loss we had no control over. What's really striking is that you already hold the truth somewhere inside you — that she knew you loved her — but in those moments, your mind is selectively gathering evidence against you, like a prosecutor ignoring everything else. I'm curious, if your grandmother were sitting with you right now and heard you say "I didn't do enough," what do you think she would say back to you?

client: I think she would probably say something like "don't be silly, of course you did enough" — she was always kind like that. But that's almost what makes it harder, you know? Like, I can imagine her saying it, but it doesn't actually make me feel it, it just feels like I'm putting words in her mouth to make myself feel better.
therapist: There's something really honest and painful in what you just shared — you're almost distrusting your own comfort, as if allowing yourself to feel better would somehow be cheating or not "real." But I'd gently invite you to consider: the fact that you can so naturally and specifically hear her voice saying those kind words — that kindness, that "don't be silly" — where do you think that comes from, if not from genuinely knowing her and the love that was real between you? What do you think it would mean for you if you allowed yourself to actually receive that comfort, even just a little?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're right — that I wouldn't be able to hear her voice so clearly if it wasn't real. But there's this other part of me that feels like if I let myself feel comforted, it means I'm okay with her being gone, and I'm really not okay with it. It's like accepting the comfort feels like accepting the loss, and I don't know if I'm ready to do that yet.
therapist: What you just named is such a profound and important insight — that receiving comfort feels like it might mean surrendering your grief, as if letting go of the pain is somehow letting go of her. But I want to gently offer another way to look at it: comfort and grief aren't opposites, and you can hold both at the same time — the sadness of losing her *and* the warmth of knowing you were loved by her. What if staying connected to her didn't have to mean staying in the pain, but could also live in those moments of warmth you shared?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible, but it feels almost too neat, like a nice idea that doesn't quite match how grief actually works in my chest at 2am. When I try to think about the warm memories, they almost immediately get swallowed up by this wave of "but she's gone," and the warmth turns into ache before I can even hold onto it. I guess I'm skeptical that I can just... choose to let the comfort in without it feeling like I'm somehow betraying how much I miss her.
therapist: What you're describing — that warmth slipping into ache before you can even hold it — that's not a failure of thinking, that's just honest grief, and it deserves to be respected rather than rushed. And I want to be clear: I'm not suggesting you choose comfort *instead* of missing her, because that missing is actually a form of love, and there's nothing to betray there. I'm wondering though — when you imagine someone who loved their grandmother just as deeply as you did, would you tell them that feeling moments of warmth means they don't truly miss her?

client: I mean... no, I wouldn't tell them that. I'd probably say it's okay to smile when you remember someone you loved. But it feels different when it's me — like I'm supposed to know better, or hold the grief more carefully, and any moment of warmth feels like I'm already starting to forget her.
therapist: There's something really tender in that double standard you just noticed — the compassion you'd so readily offer someone else, but find almost impossible to turn toward yourself. And that fear of forgetting her... I wonder if it's actually evidence of the opposite — that someone who truly didn't care wouldn't be guarding the memory so carefully. What do you think it would take for you to trust that remembering her warmly and remembering her *fully* could be the same thing?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's true — that holding onto the grief is actually proof that I loved her, not that I failed her. But there's this voice in my head that says if I start remembering the good times without the guilt attached, I'm somehow letting myself off the hook too easily. Like the guilt is the price I have to keep paying, and if I stop paying it, it means I didn't love her enough.
therapist: That belief — that guilt is the price of love — is such a painful and common trap grief pulls us into, and it's worth really examining: did your grandmother ever make you *earn* her love by suffering? Because what you've described of her — that warm "don't be silly" — sounds like someone who loved you freely, not as a transaction. I'm curious, do you think she would actually want the price of her memory to be your ongoing pain?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, because no, she never made me earn anything. She was just... warm, you know, unconditionally. But it still feels like if I let go of the guilt, I'm somehow letting go of her too, like the pain is the last thread connecting me to her.
therapist: That image of the guilt being the last thread connecting you to her is so beautifully honest, and it tells me how deeply you're trying to hold onto her — but I want to gently ask: is the pain really the thread, or is *she* the thread? Because everything you've shared today — the way you hear her voice, the coffee shop she loved, knowing she was unconditionally warm — that's not guilt, that's her, still present in you. What if the real connection to her has been here all along, in the love itself rather than the suffering?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but it feels almost too easy, like if I just let the guilt go, I'm somehow saying it was okay that I wasn't there when she died. The love feels real, yeah, but it's all tangled up with the regret, and I don't know how to separate them without feeling like I'm letting her down again. Does that make sense, or am I just making excuses to keep punishing myself?
therapist: It makes complete sense, and asking that question — "am I punishing myself?" — takes real courage and self-awareness, so please don't dismiss it. The guilt and love being tangled together isn't something you just think your way out of neatly, and I want you to know that untangling them isn't about saying "it was okay" — it's about recognizing that you were a loving grandchild living a human life, not someone who failed her. I'm wondering, when you imagine "letting her down," what specifically do you picture — what would that actually look like to you?

client: When I imagine letting her down, I picture her last few weeks and how I kept telling myself I'd visit more, but I was busy with work and... I just didn't. Like, she died and I wasn't there enough at the end, and I think she must have felt alone, and that image just won't leave me alone. It's the specific thought that she needed me and I chose other things instead, and I can't seem to argue myself out of it no matter how hard I try.
therapist: That image sounds like it's become a kind of fixed story in your mind — "she was alone and I chose other things" — and I can hear how much it haunts you, sitting with it quietly but persistently. I want to gently ask: do you actually *know* she felt alone, or is that something your grieving mind has filled in, because the uncertainty of not knowing feels unbearable? And I'm also curious — what do you know about those last weeks that might not fit that story, even small things?
